utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday you mentioned Hrasnica. You said that it was swarming with soldiers. Do you know what was the head count of the 104th Brigade run by Fikret Prevljak and what was its lethal power?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As regards the information about this area, it was well-known. The situation in that area was well-known. Regarding your statement that the area was swarming with troops, that was a problem that was not of a major importance to us. The movements of the troops who do not open fire were not a priority problem for us. Obviously movements, manoeuvres, and any such actions are of some importance; however, there was another aspect and another type of activities that posed a greater danger to us. This boils down to several procedures which could not be tolerated. That means that infantry and artillery held under control or under fire various areas in the Sarajevo region. I'm talking about the village of Grlica, the village of Vojkovici, parts of Gornji Kotorac, and also one part of the territory of Ilidza. I'm coming back to the area and to that axis that we are discussing at the moment and this is the axis leading from Hrasnica to the slopes of Mount Igman in the direction of the battalion that was in charge of the defence in the Nedzarici sector. The essence of their intense activities and their constant movements and their abuses was in opening fire on the small village of Grlica. I don't know why the village is called that way. And very often, perhaps not every day, but very often civilians who were going about their business got killed there every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Grlica. Let me just clarify for the participants in this trial. Is Grlica a type of dove, a small dove?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that's that important. I'm not saying it's a dove. It's a bird in any case. Grlica is a bird.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often did they open fire and from what localities? I'm talking about the 104th Brigade. How often they opened fire on the parts of the Serb Sarajevo that you mentioned in your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer, I did not mention how they opened fire on the Famos factory in Sarajevo. One part of that factory was occupied by the units of the 1st Corps in initial struggle, and most of that factory was on the part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and it was in production. That factory was to be destroyed. One part of the factory was burnt to the ground. It produced gearboxes for certain types of vehicles. And then they continued to open fire on the remainder of the factory that was still intact. As far as defence goes, on one side of the factory were the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and on the other side of the wall there were others. There was practically no distance between them. On the other side of the wall were the units of the 104th Motorised Brigade. I said yesterday that that brigade had at its disposal many more lethal weapons than the other brigades in the 12th Corps. They had a contingent of 180- [as interpreted] and 82-millimetre mortars. They had 76-millimetre cannons, so-called ZIS cannons. They had a large number of recoilless guns and anti-aircraft mortars, 20/1, which means a one-barrelled cannon, and 20/3, which is a three-barrelled cannon. That would be the number of assets and weapons from which they could open fire as they willed because they had that contingent of weapons and they -- good position, an elevated position, from which they could open fire on the areas that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. You mentioned that that looked like a close contact struggle because there was practically no distance between them, but that was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but the transcript, page 3, line 9, reads "180- and 82-millimetre mortars," and perhaps -- and I suspect the General didn't mean 180-millimetre mortars which to my knowledge don't exist. Perhaps he could be asked to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a word comes out of one's mouth and it has nothing to do with reality, it cannot be valid. I don't know how this number, 180, came up, why I said that. But it was not that figure, obviously. I wanted to say 120-millimetre mortars and 82-millimetre mortars. I wanted to say what I knew that they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the last question of Mr. Karadzic's or shall I ask him to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be grateful if the question was repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, it was not recorded that you said that they were on both sides of the wall. They were at close quarters. There was no distance between them.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I understand. I can clarify possibly. On that stretch, or rather, in that whole area of struggle or the area of contact they were not close. They were at close quarters. It was not any other category of fighting that may take place in a conflict. That will be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the confrontation line went through the factory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you destroy the part that was under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was it that you became fully aware of the infrastructure of the power and the deployment of the 104th Brigade and its firing positions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that my predecessors - and I'm talking about General Galic and the commanders who were in charge of the Ilidza Brigade and the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade - I knew that they had the same feeling, that they were aware of the same fact from the very beginning of the conflict. However, they -- their power continued to grow over a period of time, I would say, and this is something that I am certain of. However, I'm not claiming that for a fact here. I don't have that possibility. Fikret Prevljak was the commander of that brigade at one time. Later on he left to become the commander of the 12th Division. I felt and we actually concluded that if a professional is not in command of an area, somebody like a career officer, then we had a lot more problems with the troops on the ground because there are no rules. I also know that Mr. Fikret Prevljak was at odds with UNPROFOR. He even planted mines on General Gobillard's route. They were removed. I would like to add to (redacted) (redacted) although he explained to Colonel Radojcic what things he experienced at the hand of Mr. Fikret. My conclusion at this place on this occasion, which I arrived at earlier on, is that the tensions, the feelings, and the ideas as to how to conduct fighting with us, how to engage us, is something that he inherited from his predecessors in a very dirty way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um, and I think lines 24 and 25 as well because that kind of signals the reasons why we might be redacting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please give us the names of some firing positions and their localities in the field itself and particularly on Mount Igman above Hrasnica. Where was fire opened from at us? What was in the centre of Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija, the entire locality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully understand your question. First of all, let's talk about the locality of Hrasnica as a neighbourhood. Hrasnica is a very large neighbourhood. Let's remind ourselves of its appearance. According to what we knew, according to what we established, that neighbourhood was covered in totality by the forces that were deployed, either by the forces that opened fire from within or that were on furlough there or reservists who were on standby to be used on a given axis. The locality itself, the area, the territory of the neighbourhood was encumbered by the military factor and the artillery assets, i.e., mortars, 120-millimetres, which opened fire from that area, as I have already told you. Furthermore, the slopes of Mount Igman, in this case the eastern slopes of Mount Igman which tower over the area that I have been talking about, which is Vojkovici, Grlica, Kotorac, and one part of Lukavica and finally one part of Dobrinja, those slopes are conducive to direct fire. They enable opening direct fire which excludes the use of calculations or a team in charge of fire. The marksman is given co-ordinates and can open fire directly. The entire road leading from Hrasnica further up towards Igman and further afield along the front line were covered on the left and on the right by assets which allegedly were deployed to protect convoys and their troops pulling out. But I would say that they opened fire at us without any necessity to do so, without any -- respecting any rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, please forgive me for not being clear enough. I always include Sokolovic Kolonija and Butmir in my question when discussing Hrasnica. Was this a single space, a single area; and if you can, tell us which units were in Sokolovic Kolonija and Butmir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a battalion in Sokolovic Kolonija which -- out of the five they had. Another one was in Butmir. So they had a battalion of soldiers that was positioned in Sokolovic Kolonija. You understood properly the setting. It is true that Sokolovic Kolonija was the kind of location which -- from which the forces of the SRK at Ilidza could be threatened. So it was turned towards Ilidza, given its close proximity. From Ilidza to Hrasnica, one needs to go through Sokolovic Kolonija first. It was a threat to the area held by the Ilidza Brigade which was close to the sports centre and the swimming pool and the spa area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What can you tell us about Donji Kotorac and Butmir? Who controlled it, what assets they had, and how distant were they from our lands and the airport?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is this: First of all, they weren't too far away from the airport. I can't say precisely what the distance was, perhaps a thousand metres, but I never gave it much thought. I simply knew it was close. Donji Kotorac and Butmir are close to the airport. Donji Kotorac and the distance between Butmir and Donji Kotorac is the area which was an open space that our forces couldn't use. If we were to discuss the issue of the siege of Sarajevo, in that direction the encirclement was not complete. There was a way out of Sarajevo in the sense that no forces of ours were there. The space is some 1.000 metres between Kotorac and Butmir. It is all further afield from the airport and they controlled it. They used it normally and it was all in the valley of the Zeljeznica river.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, in your order of the 6th of April, which is P01201, you say that targets should be chosen in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Kolonija as being the most profitable, causing the greatest material damage and loss in terms of personnel. Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica, were they equally important as military targets? And can you tell us what did you want to say when you said that greatest losses should be inflicted in terms of human casualties, who did you mean? Do you want us to recall the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it before me. I will do my utmost and tell the Chamber the following. I believed one needn't ponder much further when I state, for example, that greatest human and material losses should be inflicted. Under no conditions and in no one's mind there should be a conclusion that it was our wish or intention or that it could have pertained to civilians. If one were aware of the extent of coverage they had in that area and the amount of assets they had there, it would be clear. All I had in mind were military targets. It was superfluous -- it would have been superfluous of me to tell the brigade commander in charge to provide any further instruction or detail or description of what I meant in terms of the target we wanted to hit. It was simply military parlance. There was no other target. There's only a military target. A civilian cannot be a target; they're simply not treated as targets. They're no threat to our activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the artilleryman that the order was issued to, could he have understood it in any different way as if you were asking him to inflict civilian losses? This was, in fact, sent to the brigade commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the document was drafted -- it was sent to the brigade commander, but the document was prepared and drafted by the chief of artillery, Colonel Tadija Manojlovic, and I signed it. He brought the document to me, and when I read it, I found nothing of importance to correct in terms of content because we were in perfect understanding. I asked him whether he meant only such targets which opened fire and we agreed that the document should remain as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, how do we know that it was Tadija Manojlovic who drafted the document? Can we see it anywhere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should be, yes, MT. That is the creator of the document. RM stands for the stenographer or the dactylographer, the person who typed it up. It's just above my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D7719 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This incident found its way in your indictment as well as your judgement; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How is this incident treated by UNPROFOR? Was there a protest or was there an investigation? Was anything done at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that now. I really can't recall what the procedure was in terms of reacting to it or any investigations. I only recall that -- how things developed in my trial. Yes, I tried to explain to my counsel the sense or the meaning of the phrase "choose a target." I provided him with sufficient information in order to represent me appropriately. I really do not recall what went on in terms of any investigations or UNPROFOR reactions and everything that resulted from it. I do know, though, that in the area, due to the impact of the aerial bomb, an elderly person was killed. And some of the people who were there in the immediate vicinity, in terms of observers and UNPROFOR personnel, they had their own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether there was a significant military target close by in the area where the aerial bomb fell?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the observers stated as well. In the immediate vicinity there were artillery pieces, such as 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Aleksa Santic school, is it close by, and what do you know about what was in the building of the school during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Aleksa Santic school is where some type of manufacture took place of lethal assets for the needs of the units. Hrasnica received certain materiel that could be turned into lethal assets as they were being transported in and out of the city. I know they produced certain kind of ammunition such as hand-grenades and rifle grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, this report is dated the 8th of April but refers to the 7th of April, 1995, that's what we see on page 1. Can we go to page 2. It is an UNPROFOR report rather than an UNMO report. Kindly listen to me. I'll read it out in English. I'll read out item 2. [In English] "Central and Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] And you will receive interpretation. [In English] "Central and Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina: "(a) Sector Sarajevo: The situation is assessed to remain stable. The level of firing incidents will likely continue to rise. The rocket which impacted in Hrasnica was most likely retaliation for the mortar round fired from Hrasnica some minutes before." [Interpretation] What do you think of this report? Is it accurate? Did they inform their superiors truthfully?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is accurate. I think, sitting here, that this assertion by UNPROFOR is something that did not come up during my trial. That was the first thing I wanted to say. I know what the observers had said, but this doesn't ring a bell. My counsel did not have occasion to lead this in the courtroom as to what was the reason for opening fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2817, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you mentioned today that on both sides of the so-called Igman route or Igman road there were military facilities, units, and firing positions. A witness here told us at page 8012 - I'll read it out in English again so as to have a better interpretation. [In English] "The Igman mount road was being used by civilians to go in and out of the town. The Serbs had been engaging the route. We had protested against the Serbs from engaging that route." [Interpretation] What was the Igman road used for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The extent of my knowledge is based on what we could observe and monitor on a daily basis. We followed the route and that direction up Mount Igman. It was primarily used for military needs. It was used primarily to move columns, to bring in weapons, equipment, and supplies to Hrasnica. To us that road was of military importance and of a military nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you know, General, that it was used for military supply and unit movement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could clearly observe that. It was obvious, I'd say. One could differentiate between a civilian and a military column, including vehicles and people. When it happened that they had a military column going that way, just before they would try to create a smoke-screen. They would activate some kind of asset to create a smoke-screen in order to prevent us from realising that it was a military column. Nothing similar happened when civilians moved about. They clearly identified it for us what they did at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how were things during the night when it comes to the use of that road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was the same as it was during the day. During the night one could see the headlights well. However, night movements were not what we were interested in and we never opened fire on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was a witness who mentioned on pages 8080 and 8081 an incident and the fact that you reported to the Main Staff that the UNPROFOR had gotten involved in the conflict and that they opened fire. Can you briefly tell us whether you remember that incident and how it came about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. This is correct. UNPROFOR -- and I don't know what the intention was, whether there was co-ordination among the troops of UNPROFOR, but in any case they found themselves in the parts of the column in order to serve as their cover-up and thwart our fire, given the fact that we were never supposed to open fire on them, whatever they may have been involved in. However, they did not get involved only to provide cover but they also opened fire on us. As a result, we considered them a target like we would any other force that opened fire on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D40604, it concerns Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Earlier today you said that they used the area and that they used the road for bringing the troops in and out and for bringing in supplies. You said that it was easy to deliver supplies and combat assets and equipment into Hrasnica. What do you know about those assets and supplies, how did they arrive in the city? The number is 1D40604. Do you remember the question, General, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you remember when the tunnel was opened? Do you remember whether this transfer took place even before the tunnel was opened, although you may have not been there at the time? First of all, tell us about the document, what is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the date and the contents of the document, I have to say that I was there, I was the commander of the 1st Romanija Brigade, so that period is related to me in one way or another. First of all, the tunnel was opened and became operational in 1993, and the document speaks about activities that were going on in 1992. In any case, those assets were transferred through the airport. There was no other way. There was no other route. I've never seen this order before. At that time they could not transport anything through the tunnel; they could only do it via the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does this tally with your experience regarding the transport of assets and equipment into the city itself? Can you please clarify this, why would they need 100-millimetre projectile for a tank? Why did they need projectiles for self-propelled anti-aircraft gun in the city itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only share my thoughts. If assets are brought in such as ammunition and other equipments, that means that they had the assets that were necessary to open fire on us. The conflict had already started and this is the conflict that we have been talking about all the time. This shows that they had available assets inside and the document here speaks about resupplying ammunition for those combat assets that were in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe - if I may - the way for Dr. Karadzic to deal with documents like this is to establish some foundation first before he then shows him the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to make any observation in response to Ms. Edgerton's observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't think that that has been the practice that the Prosecution used during its direct examination and I don't think that that is required and also I don't think that affects the issue of whether the document is admissible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add, I believe that I did lay the foundation. I reminded the witness of what he had already said. He said that supplies arrived in Hrasnica and then I asked him whether those supplies were then transferred from Hrasnica into the city and then he answered. This document only illustrates things that he already spoke about, that he already testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just -- but further, Your Honour, this is about leading the witness and to -- and in line of -- in line with the guide-lines Your Honours had suggested some time ago, I think it would and -- it would be appropriate for Dr. Karadzic to, rather than lead the witness with the document, establish some manner of foundation, ask him what he knows, and then show the document to him, which would then not be leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not deal with a supply of ammunition or weapons into Sarajevo before putting this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so in different ways, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the -- I agree in principle with what Ms. Edgerton says, but you may find it of use because if you establish the ground before, it concentrates the witness's mind nicely on the issue and most likely produce a shorter, more succinct answer, which is going to take less of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2818, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I'm trying to keep things short. I am mindful of the time. Sometimes it backfires.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, earlier today I asked you where you became aware of the infrastructure and firing positions in Sokolovic Kolonija, Stojcevac, Butmir, and other areas within your zone of responsibility. I am interested in Sokolovic Kolonija, Hrasnica, and Butmir, i.e., those parts which were south of your zone of responsibility. Just a while ago you said that fire was opened almost daily. I want to show you a document which was signed by somebody on your behalf. It is 1D8006. There is an obvious mistake when you look at the stamp on the last page. The year depicted on the stamp is 1993, whereas in the heading it's the year 1992. Let's see who signed on behalf of General Milosevic and let us also look at the stamp where you will see that the year was 1993, not 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that when it was sent from the printer it was in 1993, whereas in the heading I did see that the year was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we're here, could you please look at bullet point 7 and could you please tell us what losses you suffered on that day. You don't have to read. You just tell us what losses you suffered on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under losses or casualties there is a division into those who were killed, those who were wounded, and the wounded were then divided into those who were seriously wounded, on the one hand, and those who were slightly wounded, on the other hand. There are also the names of -- first of the person who died and the unit that he belonged to and everything else, and the same applies to the wounded, their names, their units, whether they were seriously wounded or slightly wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, there is a description of places from which fire was opened at us. Could you please read that paragraph. Where was fire opened from and what were the effects of that fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Sokolovic Kolonija, Stojcevac, Butmir, Stupsko Brdo, Hladnjaca, from infantry weapons, snipers, 82- and 120-millimetre mortars, on Ilidza. Now I'm reading the localities on which fire was opened, Ilidza; Doglodi, which is a village; Luzane, which is a part of Ilidza, a residential part of Ilidza. There were two seriously wounded fighters, three slightly wounded fighters, and three civilians. In this case the civilians were wounded as well and so were my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say that all of that was the area bordering on Ilidza and the Ilidza Brigade and that's where fire came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often were such incidents described in your reports?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often, very often. Reports show that. You can see everything from reports. You can see what happened on a certain day, and in this case I can only confirm that a writing of these reports and their analysis, the analysis of what was happening on a daily basis served as information as to what were the enemy's intentions towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this says that this is the situation as it was at 1700 hours. How often -- how frequently did you send those daily reports? Should one expect another report to have been issued on the same day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on that day but there could have been an interim combat report. This is a regular combat report which provides the information about the situation of the past 24 hours. However, any incidents that may have happened in the meantime, grave incidents, new situations, are included in an interim report which is sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2819, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7514.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report which was sent on the 16th of July, 1993, at 1700 hours. Could you please tell us where was fire opened on that day? We can all read it, but let's look at the bullet point starting with 2305 hours from the Visoko direction and at 2300 hours, Sokolje, and so on and so forth. Could you please read bullet point 1 before bullet point 2.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here information on the enemy. In a nutshell, it says that the enemy was very active in the zones of responsibility. The report goes on to mention the axis, the axis of the Igman Brigade, the Ilijas Brigade, the Vogosca Tactical Group, that tactical group later on changed its name and it was no longer a tactical group, it was the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade. Within that tactical group, there was the Kosevo Brigade and there was all -- there is also an indicator pointing to the fact that there was the 1st Romanija Brigade and the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. So the first bullet point shows the axis and the deployment of forces and then it reports on their activities, mentioning the times when fire was opened, either during the day or during the night. In this case, I would say that there are details of that fire, where it was opened, and how strong it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What we are missing in the transcript is that their activities were recorded by the minutes as well. We see sometimes in the report such as 2130, et cetera. Was such detail required of your analysis, always to record the exact time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also see here that the enemy forces, with the assistance of UNPROFOR, crossed over the airport runway, moving towards Butmir and Sokolovic Kolonija. It is visible movement given the proximity of the Ilidza Brigade forces. They could see such movement and could see that UNPROFOR tolerated it. Although the airport had not been handed over to that end, it was to be used for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go down to the bottom of the page so as to see whether it's your signature. And can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2820, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D32000. 1D32000. This doesn't seem to be it. 1D32000. No -- yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So as not to waste time, General, sir, kindly introduced -- introduce the fourth, or rather, the penultimate bullet point in item 1: "At around 1245 ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fourth item?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The fourth bullet point of item 1. How many Muslim soldiers were moving about from Sokolovic Kolonija or to Sokolovic Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "At around 1245 ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand. It's not the fourth row. I was looking for the fourth row. You say "bullet point." I wasn't aware of that. Sorry. "At about 1245 about some 300 Turks moved from Hrasnica to Sokolovic Kolonija and groups of motor vehicles came from the direction of Igman to Hrasnica on several occasions." So this movement was detected and the forces specified as well as their direction. We have this estimate of 300 people, which is a force of respectable size, moving in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: By the way, you didn't sign it, someone else did. Perhaps you can tell us who, or rather, whether it was you or not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I provide an explanation regarding the signature? Authorised personnel could sign documents, but they should note that they were acting on behalf of someone else because the person authorised to issue such orders happens to be absent at that moment, whereas the person who signed it had the authority to do it in the other person's stead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at item 8. It refers to an estimate by your side as to what that kind of movement could mean.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meaning is clear. It was our conclusion because any observed event needs to be interpreted by our side and what it means for us. It was our conclusion that they were grouping forces in the area of Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija and Stojcevac. The concentration of their forces meant something to us, either they were preparing an attack or some other kind of activity. In any case, we had to be aware of it. It should not go unnoticed and without an adequate interpretation by our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a brief lexical reference. How did we call those Serbs who were converted to Islam, who became Turks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How we referred to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The word in the first line.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what you're referring to. I was never in favour of labelling anyone. They were our enemy and that's what the document should have stated. Perhaps words were used that were not necessary and I was against that. I never supported such practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in addition to this term there was a derogatory term for Muslims and do you know what it was or is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was referring to. I do know of the term but I don't want to utter it even if it were in the document. I think they were referred to as "balijas," although I have no clue what it actually means, or this word "poturice," or "Turks." I remember someone asking: What are Turkish people doing in Bosnia? It seemed to have been an intelligent person to put that question. It wasn't fair on our part to use such words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for record, could you read out paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you zoom in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or if you agree, Ms. Edgerton, that the "read" should read "real."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is a issue with interpretation. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It is noteworthy that the Turks are concentrating forces in the Hrasnica-Sokolovic Kolonija sector amounting to a realistic attack on the positions of the Ilidza Brigade ."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2821, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D32003. We'll skip some documents as we don't have enough time to go through each and every report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, it is a regular combat report issued at 5.00 p.m., referring to the 10th of August, 1993. The second paragraph, where it refers to the sports centre, could you read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2: "The units engaged" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, the bullet point: "From the sports centre."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From the Hrasnica sports centre, during the day, a 20-millimetre gun fired four shells in the area of our positions as well as one shell from the 82-millimetre mortar." The next bullet point: "Throughout the day the enemy opened sniper fire on Grbavica, Lukavica, Dobrinja, and Vojkovici."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where is the Hrasnica sports centre and was it the only instance of fire being opened from the Hrasnica sports centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in Hrasnica itself. It is a location in Hrasnica on its eastern side, unless I have forgotten some things in the meantime. I know where it is because they had the Famos football club which existed there and enjoyed quite good ratings. It was in a lower-rank league level of competition, but it is in any case in Hrasnica, close to the railroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The document's authentic, Your Honours. On that basis, I don't have a problem with it coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2822 , Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The last document from this batch of reports is 1D7517.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the document is dated the 6th of November, 1994, by which time you had already become the corps commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second bullet point in item 2: "In the area of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade ..." and so on and so forth. Can you read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear with me. This item indicates the degree of threat for the Ilidza Brigade and the territory of Ilidza municipality. Since the first part refers to activity coming from the direction of Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija, it goes on -- or rather, it's the same commander confirming what kind of activity was in his area of Brijesce, just further afield from Rajlovac. It was relatively close and from there they could engage Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you retaliate by firing an aerial bomb in this situation? Or in the previous case when they opened fire from the sports centre, did you launch an aerial bomb?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you retaliate against the firing positions where the fire had come from at Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija and the sports centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did return fire concerning the instance involving Hrasnica that we had on the screen, but whether it was on this specific date, I can't confirm that at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, the item number 2, "Our forces," please read out the first five or six lines. Perhaps you can start from the sentence: "In the area of the Nisic plateau ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "In the area of the Nisic plateau during the day there was fierce fighting along the entire front line" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... due to strong artillery and infantry fire, our forces were forced to retreat repeatedly. By 4 p.m. they were at the line Bibici village - Gradina," and we have the trig point, 1121, "Nanici - Borak" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's fine. We don't need all the locations. What does it mean due to strong artillery and infantry fire and their superiority in the field?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's logical, the logic being that no one can attempt a breakthrough by using infantry along an axis unless they have strong artillery support. It is a precondition for any infantry advance. In this case, we established that the enemy force was of such high morale and supported by their artillery so that we had to use ours to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did the offensive at the Nisic plateau begin? This is dated the 6th or 5th of May [as interpreted], but when did the fighting start?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to provide information and indicators showing their decision to engage in offensive action in the second half of the year. But, to be more precise, on the 1st of August, the 1st Corps achieved success in Nisic. On the 1st of August, via the village of Brgule, which was a Serbian village -- I'm telling you what the axis was because their movements started from Dastanjsko, all this was in the wider area of the mountain. So from there, they were firing from Brgule part of the Niksic plateau and they took part of the territory on the 1st of August, as I've already said. In their first regrouping and when they prepared additionally, they continued this activity, which you can see here took place in November. This was a fierce attack and they arrived close to a line running from Olovo to Sarajevo. And for their television, they reported on television that they had already broken through to Nisic and arrived there, but that was not true because we managed to stop them. We invested a huge effort and managed to stop them there, and that's where the line remained until the end of the war. We were at threat, the threat was enormous. There would have been no further resistance and they would have managed to breakthrough to Vogosca and join their forces in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 19, page 26, it's not the 5th or 6th of May but the 5th or 6th of November. Can we go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what does this mean: "IKM Nisici village"? And who was there at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clear, of course. "IKM" means "forward command post." What was the problem for the command there and for the functioning of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was that we had to have part of our forces to monitor the situation and to command the corps. Part of that had to be in Nisici and the other part in -- another part in Trnovo. And the rest of the command was in Lukavica. The commander was duty-bound to be either at a forward command post himself or to have his Chief of Staff or chief operations officer on the ground there in order to command the forces and make sure that the enemy did not break through due to poor command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Please can you give us brief replies because the Chamber already knows a lot about how the army functioned. Can you tell us who was at this forward command post at Nisici at the time we're referring to, in November 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you let me look at the signature, I'll tell you who it was. You see, the document was processed. I was at Nisici at the time because it's not signed because I couldn't be in the operations room to sign this myself, but I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2823, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly look at P2420, Exhibit P2420. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the first sentence says that there was information that the civil authorities met the commander, that was on the 7th of November, and that they met on the 5th of November. So in view of the fact that you were at Nisici, what can you tell us about this document? Did a meeting take place and did you attend it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I am certain that this is fabricated. I don't know for what reason. I have no idea why somebody would want to invent such a document, but I can affirm that I never had any kind of meeting with the civil authorities, let alone a meeting at which the use of certain units in combat was discussed. I reject this totally. And I know that the OTP conducted an investigation and interviewed Mr. Prstojevic, the president of Ilidza municipality, as a person who was one of the leaders at the time, and he also stated that this meeting was never held, that he knew nothing about it. And he also stated that what it says here, that I discussed things with someone else, that he thought that I, as a normal person, would never agree to what is described here. And this is in the interview between the OTP investigator and that gentleman, but the record of this interview never arrived here at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break another question. Was your command ever influenced by the civilian authorities and especially the SDS or its leaders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they had no influence whatsoever on my work. My understanding was that the civil authorities understood that they were unavailable to influence me, not because they were prevented from doing their work but because they saw that it would not be rational or intelligent to try. When it comes to imposing standpoints and so on, they refrained from that sort of thing. They didn't become involved in that. I am glad that they took my requests into account. Of course I did have to have certain contacts with them, but it's well-known that the army can only deal with army matters and not engage in political affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the civil authorities of Republika Srpska, did they interfere in purely military matters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I never experienced that from any person or structure of the government, either through any activities carried on by the cabinet or the Presidency. We never had an opportunity to meet; but when we did meet, we never discussed combat activities to be carried out by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And the politics never influenced the military situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it the right time for a break, Your Excellencies, or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we break, can we see the previous document again, Exhibit D2823. General, if we see the first page of this document, we know that it was sent by SRK to the various units, such as Main Staff, Herzegovina Corps, Drina Corps, and the forward command post in Nisic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, you are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how do we know that it was sent from the IKM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was not sent from the forward command post. It was sent from the command, and it says here that a copy was sent to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you said we can know that by this document you were in Nisici at the time. Could you explain a bit further how we can know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For me as the commander to know what the contents of the message were that was sent to the Main Staff after the document was processed, it -- from the forward command post the document was sent to the operations centre, and then in the operations centre all the documents were brought together and compiled into a single document. And then a copy was sent to me for me to see what was actually forwarded to the Main Staff. So that was one reason. Secondly, as I know that because of the threat when the 1st Romanija Corps and some of the forces were at great risk, as soon as I received the information about the combat activities and the breakthroughs, I had to be there and I was there, I did go there. And on my honour, I confirm that I was there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it says -- it was omitted in the interpretation that the General said: I was unable to sign. Maybe he could explain why he was unable to sign the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said that in his earlier answer. For planning purposes, how much longer do you need, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least by the end of today. I hope I'll be finished today. If I ask the General to make his responses very brief, although his exhaustive replies are useful, if I can get succinct replies I will be finished today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.06.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the use of snipers is very prominent in the indictment against me. I have to ask you, in general terms, a very general question: What is a sniper in a military formation and how is it used? What is a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A sniper rifle is an infantry weapon. It is used by the infantry. As a matter of fact, we had sniper rifles, 7.9-millimetres, M76. Its calibre was 7.9, as I've already told you. That rifle fired sniper ammunition and optical sights for spotting targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say "sniper rifle ammunition," would you say that this differs from other 7.9-calibre ammunition and especially from the 7.62-millimetre automatic rifle ammunition?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a difference, absolutely. You cannot use the same type of ammunition in a sniper rifle of 7.9-calibre. You cannot use the same calibre ammunition that is intended for other types of weapons. A sniper rifle has its own sniper rifle ammunition. I'll try and be succinct in providing my answer. Maybe this was already enough. In any case, my defence counsel could not distinguish between those two things, so when the Prosecutor put to him: See how much 7.9-calibre ammunition you order and that was to be used in sniper rifles, I tried to explain to him that that ammunition could not be used in sniper rifles and that the quantities ordered could not be used in evidence that that ammunition was used by sniper rifles. I could not explain that to him and he never used my argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please remind us what other purposes does the 7.9-millimetre ammunition have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be used for the rifle M48. This is an old type of rifle that was used by the JNA and that was part of the armament of our army, the Army of Republika Srpska. Furthermore, a machine-gun can also use 7.9-millimetre ammunition, and I believe that the story ends there. I don't want to go into any other types of ammunition, such as Zbrojovka. The most important types of weapons are the two that I mentioned at the beginning of my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of fire was opened by machine-guns and what is the average consumption of ammunition? Can bursts of fire be opened? How many rounds does a machine-gun use?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: M42 machine-guns are automatic weapons with high velocity. It has a belt. I can't remember the velocity of firing, but those bursts of fire cannot be compared with the fire opened by a sniper rifle because a sniper rifle can fire only individual bullets. And another thing that I've not explained so far is the fact that the sniper rifle is a semi-automatic rifle so it cannot fire bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, if somebody was hit by a single bullet which was part of a burst of fire, could that have been a bullet fired by a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It could not have been fired by a sniper rifle because a sniper rifle cannot fire bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether an investigation or an analysis of projectiles could yield a conclusion as to whether a bullet was fired from a sniper rifle or from an M84 or a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that it would be possible, but I'm not saying that as an expert but as a person who knows, who was told, that those are two different rounds, two different bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive an analysis as the Chief of Staff or a corps command or the results of an investigation that provided a conclusive finding as to whether a bullet was fired from a sniper rifle or from some other rifle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never in the course of the last war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In all of your units, did you have sniper rifles? Did you have them at the forward front line turned outwards and turned inwards and why did you have them? What was their intended use?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All units had sniper rifles. It was our obligation, it was our duty, to provide every combat unit with its sniper rifles and a dedicated marksman. That principle applied across the board in the entire zone of responsibility, and especially in the areas where there was a high concentration of enemy sniper rifles, that's where we had our sniper rifles and our marksmen as well. Furthermore, it was not easy to choose marksmen and it was not a simple procedure. A marksman had to possess certain qualities. First of all, they were not supposed to have a criminal record. They could not be short-sighted and they had to be patient and they had to be trained. If they are not trained, formally trained, if they had not been trained by the JNA, their military specialty was 11-101 [as interpreted], just like any other marksman, but their military specialty was specified and they were known as marksman specialists and that was their qualification from the JNA. And then the officers would decide whether those people would be hired. Let me add to that that our soldiers did not want to be sharpshooters, given the close vicinity of the front line, the high level of danger, and especially because they placed more trust in weapons that could open bursts of fire in close contact because they were more efficient and they provided more security. Another thing was that sharpshooters were static. They had to remain in one place and they had to be very patient. They had to be very focused in order to be able to spot the enemy sharpshooter. That was their main task, to observe enemy sharpshooters. We arrived at the information that on the opposite side there was quite a lot of people who used those weapons against us and they had to be engaged. And another task of a sharpshooter was to detect other targets that may have been of significance for the enemy and for us they posed a threat; for example, other weapons or important military personnel. Let me say at the beginning of my answer that no matter who a sharpshooter was, they were never issued an order to open fire on civilians and they never did that. They were never told to do that and they never did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that your enemy on the other side had sharpshooters which opened fire. When did they first obtain sniper rifles and when were they active and where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within Sarajevo there was a special MUP brigade which was always known as the Brigade Bosna or the Bosnia Brigade. Those men were primarily trained as sniper shooters. They knew how to use sniper rifles. That was their paramount quality. Second of all, we knew that there was a group which was known as Seve. They were our archenemies. They were deployed in the school of machine engineering. They were on top of the building of the Assembly, the building of the government. They did not think twice who to shoot. They killed civilians as well. They had to be detected and that's why we had sniper shooters, to engage them. They had sniper rifles but they also had the rifles known as Dragon. I don't know what its specific characteristics were. I only know that those rifles were better than the 7.9 semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about the 5.56- or 12.7-millimetre calibre? I'm talking about the Dragon.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's 12.7, it's too large. I don't know. I don't want to speculate. I don't know much about that rifle, but I know that they had it because I was told that by others who knew more about it. I knew it was the so-called Dragon rifle.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D40665. 1D40665.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read, General, sir, I'm waiting for the English translation. The document was issued on the 6th of March, 1993. The efficient engagement of sniper shooters. And it says: Further to letter strictly confidential so and so, I hereby issue the following order. First of all, all sniper shooters in battalions should be on duty in all weather conditions whenever possible. And now the rest -- may be we can go to the following page in English. All sniper shooters have to be qualified as soldiers, sniper shooter capable of returning fire and performing tasks during night or day. Did the other side have conditions in place to use sniper rifles during night and did they indeed use them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's not about sniper fire at night. It's fire opened at night with a -- from a weapon which is not a sniper rifle. It is a rifle with a passive optical sights. Passive optical sights imply that through them you can observe targets during night and you can open fire during night as you could during the day. In any case, when it comes to sniper rifles we're talking about a different thing. Sniper rifles are one thing and passive optical sights are another thing and they're used at night. Maybe the distinction that was made here is not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about this order where it says that they should be used in all weather conditions, they should be used at all times? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that they opted for that type of fire, for that type of activity and actions, i.e., that they wanted to use those weapons all the time en masse in order to neutralise or destroy our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Sulejman Imsirevic's order carried out? Is that how they behaved? Is that what they did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events and developments on the ground confirmed that this order was implemented because we experienced that fire. That fire was as it is described in here. That fire was opened and it -- and we felt it on our own skin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask my associates to talk to the CLSS to complete the uncomplete translation, and in that respect I would like to offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is your case and the evidence of General Milosevic that the Serb forces never issued an order to open fire on civilians and that it never took place, that would be it for your defence. Why do we need this kind of evidence, i.e., the sniping on the part of Muslims, at all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, the witness gave me a reason for which he had sniper rifles. The goal was to neutralise Muslim sniper rifles in town and to neutralise other legitimate military targets. As for the Muslim sniper shooters in town and where they were employed and how they operated, this is what this document describes and confirms. They were active all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind that you were never indicted for having snipers at all. Ms. Edgerton, about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I actually don't think we know what it is, what military unit it relates to, under whose command the unit fell, what zone it operated in. We know absolutely nothing about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did the witness not confirm Sulejman Imsirevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He confirmed that -- he said in response to

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC'S QUESTION
utterances.text: "Was Mr. Imsirevic's order issued?" He said: "Yes." I don't think that satisfies any of the issues I just raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you kindly read out the title of this document because it hasn't been fully translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm providing the following answer. These are the early days of their existence and you see that their name at the time was the command of the military unit and its number was 5457, which implies that it was a military composition. Second of all, they were deciding how they would engage their manpower, how they would operate. There are no ambiguities there. However, the most important thing is that the document shows that from day one they had at their disposal this contingent of weaponry which could open fire in a certain way. So it was no novelty. Later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that they continued to operate on the same principle and that it -- that continued throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I asked you is to read the title of this document because it's not fully translated in English. The English says: "More efficient engagement of" and illegible. Engagement of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sniper shooters, snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2824, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, while you were still in command of the 1st Romanija unit, did you have information on the activity of their snipers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D7518.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is one of your documents. It is a regular combat report. The stamp reads the 25th of July, 1992. Kindly look at line 3 of item 1. "During the day the enemy continued with intensive sniper fire, engaging almost the entire line of defence of the brigade, with particularly strong fire from the IV," or Executive Council, "building, the Marsal Tito barracks and Pofalici (the wide high-rise) ..." Further below it mentions Banja Lucka Street where a soldier was killed. "The sniper fire at this point is so strong that it is virtually blocking the entry of pedestrians to the settlement of Grbavica." Do you recall this and what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it suffices for me to confirm whether what is stated in the document indeed took place. Everything developed literally the way put here, including their firing position and the area which they targeted. They influenced every aspect of life in the area. I can confirm what the document states. One could clearly observe and feel that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The wide high-rise you mentioned in Pofalici, was that a residential building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, tell us what was the position on using snipers in the city on the part of the SRK and what was the policy of the other side, that is to say, the 1st Corps of the Army of BH?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly "position"? I can specify the regulations we set in place according to which instructions were issued to our officers and snipers, their soldiers. That's what I can discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, actually I was interested in the interest of the SRK. Were you interested in maintaining and perpetuating sniper activity and what was the interest of the 1st Corps regarding the same issue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope I'll answer clearly since I'm now providing my opinion and that's what I can formulate. When we learned of their activity being used en masse and excessively, I dare say, we had to create a structure which would address that. In order to efficiently engage such opposing forces we tried to aim our activities at that but were never fully successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why were you in favour of anti-sniping agreements?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well-known once you receive such extensive activity from the other side which becomes unbearable, one looks for a way out. And it is only good that there were some sort of mediators or go-betweens who were attempting to reach an agreement. In this case, it would have made it easier on us to a certain extent and indeed the agreement was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're still on page 1, I'll read out the following and perhaps you can confirm whether I read it accurately. The diplomacy or something else and UNPROFOR for sniper cease-fire. It seems to be a handwritten remark. Is that something of yours or was it written by someone from your command who received the report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting. Yes, I'm aware of this suggestion. When I ordered that contact be established with UNPROFOR in order to raise the issue of sniper cease-fire, in particular by the other side, we had to work with them on reaching an agreement. It is not my handwriting but the suggestion is mine. We were trying basically to contact UNPROFOR through our security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 2, item 8, or maybe the last page or the third page, whatever it is in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So as not to read out the whole thing, what was your suggestion in item 8?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suggested what it says, I've been saying it all along. The intensity of sniper fire by the enemy has risen to such level where we need to come up with a solution in order to have it stopped. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did your suggestion fare? Was an agreement reached?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 14th of August, that is to say, shortly after I assumed the duty of corps commander, which was on the 10th, the agreement was reached on the 14th. It was signed at the airport. I signed for our side and Mr. Karavelic, the 1st Corps commander, signed on behalf of the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The following sentence of yours which says: As of the moment when cease-fire was announced until today we have been suffering more losses due to sniper fire than we had before the cease-fire. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is actually what happened to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did cease-fire agreements allow for sniper activity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course once there is an agreement in place it is understood not to use them. That was the agreement. One needs both sides for an agreement. You cannot agree on something unilaterally. The agreement was reached and it was a temporary cease-fire, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us why it took two years to actually implement your proposal, that is to say, that the other side would accept your proposal and that UNPROFOR would secure the implementation, why the two years?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone is aware of their reasons. I only know that it should have taken place earlier. Now, why the other side was not prepared to accept that, well, they needed the situation in which there were constant provocations in order to draw fire so that they could portray themselves as the side in danger and that they could be considered the side that is in danger by our activity, as our side being the main reason of their plight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which side are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The side where the 1st Corps was, that is to say, the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2825, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D7519.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is your regular combat report dated the 25th of July, 1992. In item 1 you say: "The enemy is continuing with intensive sniper fire ..." In the third paragraph you say: "The brigade units during the day did not engage although they were incessantly fired at from snipers." In item 5 you say: "The morale in our units remains unchanged as compared to the previous day. There are frequent violations of cease-fire by the enemy which is keeping our fighters and civilians tense around the clock. We demand that UNPROFOR be informed."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing else to say, other than it was an indication that we were looking for a way out, even communicating with some other factors who could restrain the enemy side in this activity of theirs. In this particular instance, the sniping was so threatening that the entire issue of waging war any further came into question because one cannot survive long under such circumstances and we had to come up with someone to protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in item 5, did you enjoy any of the benefits of cease-fire on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation of the civilians and the people there in general was such that they were constantly feeling threatened, endangered. I cannot describe it fully. Perhaps I can only say that I had entire groups of people come begging for some additional protection in the areas where they lived. They thought that perhaps we could step-up our fire in order to restrain the other side. And they would tell us, for example, that the elderly people could not enjoy their senior years, their children could not enjoy their adulthood, and their grandchildren could not enjoy their childhood. We tried to convince them to the best of our power that we would try and do something, and this included engaging other instances to communicate with the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
