utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat his question. The speakers overlapped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR manage to achieve anything with regard to your pleas in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm whether they achieved anything then. I can confirm, however, that in the contacts with UNPROFOR commanders or some of their senior structures, I was happy to hear that they had a proposal which I accepted. They called it "no death day," to have a day without deaths. And they asked me if I would accept it. And my response was: Would you ask a person dying of thirst whether he wants to drink? Of course. There were requests which I accepted and I stressed that no such day can come about unless the other side honours it as well. And they said they would try to achieve that. Even if there was a day like that, the very next day people were being killed again. I believe the other side was looking for a solution as well. I accepted UNPROFOR's proposal but it didn't live too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the SRK undertake any counter-measures at a certain point, organising their own sniping unit and to what end?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the end or the aim was always the same, which was to counteract those engaging in the very same activity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2826, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P1010 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, the document is dated the 4th of November, 1992, the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. It was sent to all units. It is -- its reference line reads: "Designating locations for snipers in the zones of responsibility." It reads: "Based on reports of the commands of subordinated units on the enemy sniper activities, the identified fire positions at certain axes and the enemy troops' passages to Dobrinja from Butmir via the airport ... I hereby issue the following ..." Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not important whether I remember it or not. I know the gist or the point of this order. It was our side looking for a way to counteract their activity and to address their movements and other sorts of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I move on, do we have a permission or an order to engage civilians or to undertake any illegal activity by sniping?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is impossible. There are no circumstances or situations in which the commander at any level could even contemplate, let alone say it, to open fire at non-military targets. In this case, too, such orders could not be issued. No one would be allowed to target civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was not interpreted completely. I asked whether the preamble specifying the reasons also refers to any targeting of civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As regards the well-known sniping incidents, did anyone from the SRK take part in investigations? Were there any investigations which could conclusively find what sort of ammunition was used and what was the firing position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were always investigations in such situations when we knew what had happened, when we received information that something had happened. When we were not aware of something taking place, then no investigation was possible. What is important, though, is that when we were aware of a particular incident there was an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to participate in on-site investigations on the other side? Were you allowed to take part in order to objectively ascertain the facts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not possible, nor was it allowed. I know that the Main Staff issued a request to that effect. They wanted an investigation to be carried out by a team of people who hailed from the territory of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, or rather, those who were members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the indictment against me, several incidents are mentioned and it is claimed that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps opened sniper fire on trams and other means of public transport. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I know that this is part of your indictment. Now I hear it from you. It was also part of my indictment. I can't say anything else but that. I know that in situations when fire was opened from the other side and then we responded by fire, either cross-fire or fire opened in one direction, I know that it could happen that due to that fire bullets could also hit trams. I had information to the effect that - and I will share that with you although I could not verify that information - that citizens were told not to worry when they took trams, fire would be opened to protect you. As a result of that, citizens dared get on the trams and travel in the direction of the city. That should not have been done because when they opened fire we had to react, we had to respond by opening fire against them. And when we did that, an odd bullet could hit a tram. That's what I know from the indicators that I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D32009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your regular combat report issued on the 19th of August, 1993. And now I would like to show you the second page. We don't have the time to go through the entire document. It says here: In the course of the day, the enemy opened sniper fire on Lukavica, [indiscernible] and Vojkovici from its position and especially from Mojmilo and Dobrinja. Are these civilian settlements that are enumerated here, Grbavica, Lukavica, Nedzarici, and Vojkovici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get the following page in Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Bullet point 8. It says here: Conclusions, forecasts, and decisions. "The enemy violates the cease-fire and provokes. On the whole our forces are adhering to the cease-fire and return fire only when authorised. And now it is expected that the enemy will increase operations particularly on Sarajevo to provoke our forces into opening fire. "The enemy is continually digging in and getting closer to our lines at Stojcevac, Dobrinja, Stupsko Brdo, and Mojmilo." Would this constitute crawling towards our conditions [as interpreted] by means of digging in and digging trenches and is that allowed during a period of cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called this biting into our positions. This is a type of activity which, under the guise of reinforcing one's position, sees soldiers moving closer towards the units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which constitutes a threat to the further course of the conflict and our existence. The agreement implied that the front line would be peaceful in every aspect and at all times. It excluded anything else including additional digging in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about this, Serbs are digging in groups of 10 to 15 people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were people who found themselves in their prisons. The biggest number of people was in the silos in Tarcin, and those people were engaged to dig trenches and shelters. Those men actually constructed the tunnel under the airport. They were the ones who dug it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the last sentence says the following: "The units have been ordered to open sniper fire on targets observed" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, could we ask the General to read out that sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The units have been ordered to exclusively open sniper fire on the targets they observe that pose a threat to our soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- this word, has it been stricken through or underlined?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think I heard "samo" from the witness but it was not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the word "samo" can be interpreted as "exclusively."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, what do you think, is this word "samo" stricken through or underlined? What do you think, does this remain as part of your order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's underlined. This "samo" is underlined. It's not very clear. It's a bit badly done, but the entire sense remains as it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2827, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Given that order that you issued, would you say that this implies opening sniper fire on civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Everybody understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up 65 ter 12336.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was signed on your behalf by somebody else. We will see it on the last page. However, this is a regular combat report issued at 1700 hours on the 10th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up a little and see what it says here about the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Our units successfully repelled all enemy attacks. They responded to enemy provocations. It was the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade and the Ilijas Infantry Brigade that responded from infantry weapons and mortars as well as by opening sniper fire."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what do you expect from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I did not complete. I'm going to read slowly because we don't have an official translation. Further down it says: "Sniper fire from the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade killed two enemy soldiers. One of them was a komandir," or a commander, "the UNPROFOR soldiers have informed us about that, seeking approval to pull their bodies out." Did UNPROFOR protest therefore or did they understand that as a legitimate operation and did they ask to pull their bodies out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't -- UNPROFOR did not react adversely. They understood that fire was opened on military targets during combat. I don't see anything in dispute there, but this shows something else. Our reporting was done in the way to reflect as things really were. It -- we did not try to disguise anything. We did not try to pretend that we did not open fire when we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was strictly confidential and it was sent to the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Four days later, General, sir -- I don't know what we are looking at. I don't know what document we are looking at. I think it's 1D009. Four days later you signed an anti-sniping agreement; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am charged with your alleged control over sniping activity and when you signed that agreement the activities of Serbian sniper shooters stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get this document on the screen. It doesn't seem to have been admitted into evidence, 1D009. The following page. It's -- it's not the document I asked for. It's 1D1009. 1D1009. Agreement, yes. Can we see the following page. It says here: "Subject, agreement on elimination of sniping in Sarajevo." Page 3, can we go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you remember - can we scroll up - do you remember whether you signed this agreement two years after your first request that that agreement be signed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is obviously my handwriting in the Latinic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what was sniping fire on the Serbian side conditional upon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an elementary issue. When their sniping fire stopped, ours stopped as well. There was no need for further sniper fire. Combat could go on without opening sniper fire, without using sniper rifles. They were excluded from combat from there on. They were excluded even from hitting military targets.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted if it hasn't been admitted yet and the previous as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification, the previous document. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But this document is, I think, P861, the anti-sniping agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 12336 will be marked for identification as D2828, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P863.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Four days later you issued an order. I would like to call up P863. I don't have a Serbian version. I'm going to read it, therefore. [In English] "Pursuant to the anti-sniping agreement signed at the airport Sarajevo on the 14th of August, 1994, it was given to all troops of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps the following. "Order. "Stop immediately ... activities and activities from other weapons -- sniping activities and activities from other weapons from the front line inside the town of Sarajevo." [Interpretation] Thank you. Now bullet point 5. [In English] "It is the obligation of the commands to prevent individual unauthorised actions and irresponsible actions." [Interpretation] General, sir, you issued this order. Did the sniping activity stop after that, both from the city and from outside of the city?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it stopped. In this case, the units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps observed this agreement to the letter. That kind of fire was discontinued, obviously did not last long on the opposite side. They did not keep quiet for too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time after that when that agreement was violated on both sides? I'm talking about the agreement that was signed on the 14th of August and your order issued on the 18th of August. How long did it all last? How successful was this exercise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there is no exact date when that kind of conduct stopped and when it started again. I'm talking about violations of the agreement. So the date is not important. I don't have it in any case. In any case, as far as I can remember the cease-fire may have lasted for about a month. During that time there was no sniping activity. Sniping activities were suspended or limited. The agreement was observed and so on and so forth. And then on our side we resumed after the enemy side started opening sniper fire on us. During that period and during all the other periods in question, I confirmed that our activities against targets outside of those that you mentioned never existed, and when I say "other targets," I mean civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, after the agreement fell through, did you or anyone on the VRS side issue an order on trying to avoid sniper fire or did you prohibit opening fire at the city?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see the agreement as a complete failure. I do know that we did our utmost to honour it and to keep it in place throughout; however, it did not enjoy that status for long. As for our orders, limitations, instructions and caution, they were issued even following the violations of the agreement by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did the Serb side have a military or political interest in continuing sniper activity in Sarajevo and what was the interest of the other side? Actually, who benefitted from it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of the SRK and the position of the other forces and civilians was not such that we saw any interest in increasing that kind of activity or continuing with it in order to expand the conflict. I'm basically trying to say that it was not in our interest. I said several times that the enemy side did not see any interest in resolving the situation peacefully and we constantly felt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I wanted to ask you something about the Geneva Conventions and international humanitarian law and the laws of war and how they were respected. What can you tell us about it in terms of JNA regulation and VRS position as well as the position of the SRK in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the rules of the Geneva Conventions are very clear. There is no need to add or interpret them. Fortunately, they exist as such and no one can depart from that framework in -- absent a very solid reason to do so. The spirit of those rules was present in the mind of every member of the SRK. I repeat, the fighters and people who were under fire on a daily basis actually kept asking us why we kept bothering them by saying that they shouldn't act against civilians. Of course we clearly told them that we were not interested in civilians. We had to keep reminding them irrespective of how responsibly they approached the issue. That was one thing. Another thing, I know that we do not have enough time but I could tell you every activity and move I made together with the rest of my command in order to honour the Geneva Convention rules to the utmost. It was done in different ways. For example, in the commands of battalions, in bold letters there were such rules and it was insisted that the battalion commanders pass that information down through their company commanders and ultimately plain soldiers so that they would not commit such mistakes. That was one thing. Another thing, we were constantly in touch with many people and through that contact they were made aware of the fact that such conduct would be inhumane, it would not be chivalrous and it would be below anyone's dignity to act against the rules of the Geneva Conventions. That's all I have to say about it. Although, as I said, I could put forth a number of indicators and examples on how we worked with the people in situ. I tried every time to tell them what was important for them as participants in the war. They never heard from me or my commanders anything that would indicate that their negative conduct would be permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, given the fact that the corps command and brigade commands for the most part were comprised of professional military personnel, whereas the soldiers had served in the JNA, were your instructions their first encounter with the Geneva Conventions? What was their knowledge of the Geneva Conventions and international laws of war on the part of your commanders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders and officers were completely familiar with it. They were aware of the gist and thrust of the rules. One learns that through military education. It was so taught that no one needed any further persuasion. It was simply a rule that was there. The soldiers did receive training on that topic. I'm not asserting that we explained in every detail what would await a person going against that rule, especially in view of the fact that soldiers needn't be burdened with every single rule there was. But there was knowledge which for the most part came from the officers who were well aware of the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We had occasion to hear the testimony of several of your brigade commanders. What would be your take on the dignity, professionalism, and humaneness of your brigade commanders? Did you have any issues with any of them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very good question. I'm happy that someone is interested in how those people conducted themselves. First of all, I personally hold each and every of those commanders in high regard. They have confirmed themselves as people of military and ethical principles, aware of their knowledge and ready to apply their knowledge in order for our side not to be defeated. That's what I have to say about them. They enjoyed my trust and in turn I received theirs. Never, even in jest or when chatting, was there ever any thought or word uttered that we should do something that would be humiliating or detrimental to the level of those people who were in command of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what was the position of your predecessor, that is to say, the first commander of the SRK, General Sipcic and his commanders vis-a-vis respecting the rules of the Geneva Conventions? Did you meet with General Sipcic and did you have an opinion as regards that issue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is well-known and clear that General Sipcic was the corps commander for a very brief period of time. While he was there, I never saw him make a wrong move or a decision in that regard. His tone was not extremely commanding, but his conduct was also not detrimental to our side in any respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position concerning civilians, especially civilians of other ethnicity in the area of responsibility of your brigade and later on your corps? What kind of measures were taken to protect them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the area of the SRK, especially in its south-eastern part, there was a number of people of another ethnicity, in this case Muslims. I know that no crimes were committed against them. When you asked me earlier how we conducted our investigations, I'm pleased to know that in the area of the SRK there were no crimes such as beatings, detention, torture, mistreating, killings, et cetera. The same status was accorded to Muslims as the other citizens living in our territory. They were not tortured or approached in a negative way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the organised forces under your control and does this include individuals outside of your control?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not understand. Individuals outside my control? I don't know what it means. I am talking about the people, territory, and population in the area of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you are referring to your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about their attitude towards the civilians in our territory. There were no crimes committed against people irrespective of their ethnicity in the area of our forces and our front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did the Muslims and Croats have the same obligation to respond to call-ups like the Serbs? Did you have soldiers and officers of Muslim and Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did, especially in Grbavica. There was a number of soldiers, Muslims, who were used in combat deployment. They held the line in that area like any other soldier. They were members of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they have the same obligation, both Muslims and Croats in our territory, the same as the Serbs had to respond?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not want to force them. There was no way or means to force them to join our ranks. Those who found themselves on our territory could be engaged under work obligation. There were two categories: Military obligation and work obligation. And work obligation was something like the civilian protection, whereby people were used to work in residential areas and help other people. They were engaged in all sorts of tasks in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the corps as a whole, did you have any soldiers or officers, high-ranking officers, of a different ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. In the corps there were all ethnicities among the officers, all the ethnicities of the former Yugoslavia, that is. There were Croats who were doctors and chiefs of the medical corps -- actually, there was just one man, Colonel Tonci Posa [phoen]. We also had a colonel who was the base commander at Pale. I can't remember his name at the moment, but he was a professional, he was a very good soldier. I will remember his name. We also had Lieutenant-Colonel Milivoje Solar. He was a Croat. Together with his three daughters he spent the entire war at Grbavica. At the same time, he also got a fourth child, a son. He spent the entire war there. He was involved in logistics. There were also soldiers and -- yes, there was also Major Franc Lesnik [phoen] who was a Slovenian. I had a captain who was a Hungarian. Those people were involved in the work of the command or in the work of the units. They performed their duties as officers who knew what they were doing. They were professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question before the break. What was the attitude towards the protection of abandoned property? Did the army have anything to do with protecting the property of those who temporarily left the area, primarily the area of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a question very close to my heart, very well-known to me. I have to let you know that I can't describe everything. However, those were initial activities, initial measures that had to be introduced in order to establish some sort of order. I would like to emphasize that I was a huge advocate of order in a situation when some people did not understand what it meant to live in an area where things were still not clear enough, and this especially applies to Grbavica, to an area where from day one some people had their own agenda which they had carried over from some other times. And those activities were so frequent that I had to engage a military police company in order to reinstate order in the area and protect people. Primarily people who needed protection were Muslims who were there and who feared threats. When they realised that there was protection to be had, that somebody did not allow unknown people to enter their apartments, they were grateful. It was my company commander Djurkovic who did that. I appointed him myself. Before that he was a company commander, an active-duty officer. And when the decision was made that people should be sent to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, he left. I issued him a certificate showing how good he was in my service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you know about the position of the Main Staff, of the Supreme Command, the president of the republic, and the government with regard to your activities to the effect of preserving the lives, property, rights, and security of civilians of other ethnicities in your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position was clear and I was happy that the position was clear because it meant that people who lived there were not exposed to any sort of ill-treatment on the part of the soldiers. They accepted that protection. Second of all, the general principle and requirement was not to do evil unto others. I accepted that. Everybody was moderate in a demanding situation, so there were moderate positions by the Main Staff, by yourself, and all the other factors that constituted political power and governed the entire political situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, is this the time for our next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 22 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what measures were applied in order to curb crime in the zone of responsibility of your brigade and, later on, in the zone of responsibility of your corps? We'll see a document later.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several measures. The basic intention was to prevent their movements, especially if it was suspected that they would be able to engage in their criminal activity there. For example, in the central urban area. The key measure that I can confirm was applied on my part was to involve them in combat, to make them members of a unit and place them under a certain command. From there onwards, they stopped playing a criminal role. In other words, they were mobilised. They became members of combat teams, and they could not freely move around. And that was if they had displayed some sort of negative behaviour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7522. 1D7522. We have the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an order which was issued by the command of the 1st Romanija Brigade on the 15th of July, 1992. Somebody signed on your behalf but your name is typed up. Can you present the document to us and why you issued it. Measure to prevent theft and misappropriation of property, the introduction of a curfew. Could you please briefly tell us what prompted you to issue this document and what this document implied at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I would like to thank you for showing me this document. I completely forgot about that. These are measures that I wanted to introduce and I did introduce them because we had to curb some negative behaviours by certain factors who had not grasped the situation as it prevailed at the time. In any case, these were measures aimed at restoring order and curbing damaging behaviour, theft, burglaries, and a number of other activities that some people may have been prepared to engage in, not realising that we were in a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that ambulances were allowed to do their job. Under bullet point 2, where it says: "Measures to prevent theft and misappropriation of property." Could you please tell us whose property was mostly exposed to that type of crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were prone to property theft did not ask too many questions, but they primarily chose to steal from Muslims. The feeling that a period of lawlessness had emerged was conducive to such activities. Both the introduction of a curfew and the second measure -- let's understand each other. I didn't even know if I had the right to introduce such measures, but I didn't pay too much attention whether that was my legal obligation or not. I just needed to curb that kind of behaviour and I had to do it at the roots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that respect, General, sir, can we scroll down a little because on the top of the page we can see that something was scribbled by hand and there is a question mark. We can't see it in e-court, but let me read this to you. Somebody wrote down: "Where's the police?" And there is a question mark after those words. Where were the police at the time? Were there enough state organs, primarily courts and police, that would have allowed you not to introduce those measures?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were not enough and the police could not be efficient. Since there was a state of chaos, somebody had to take measures, and I really don't think it is important whether it was the police who did that or military organs, especially in that area that was rather small and order had to be introduced, whereas the police -- obviously the police were there but they did not function properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did someone from the Main Staff, the government, or the Presidency hold it against you, did they complain to you because you had introduced these measures?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next page and then I will ask that this part that was not visible on the screen be shown to the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it now in the English translation, yes, "where's the police." What it says here in the third and fourth line, all the property that has been stolen where the perpetrators are known has to be restored to its owners. Was this done and to what extent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course we managed to do that, but not absolutely, not everything could be detected, not everything could be discovered and restored, but for every citizen who has been robbed or looted, of course, he is happy to have his property restored and we have to make certain this doesn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was any distinction made according to ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the point, not to draw any distinctions. You have to understand that in that period we still lived in the same way as before, and those who were taking measures wanted to restore things to normal and not have individuals acting wilfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Geneva Conventions and the rules and customs of war, and this includes prisoners of war. Can you explain what you wrote under point 4, which says "treatment of prisoners of war," or rather, "procedure with prisoners," and can you tell us what you prescribed when it comes to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document and in the practice I wanted to be implemented, we wanted it to be regulated from the outset how prisoners should be treated. I don't think there's anything more just than respecting a person who has been taken prisoner. That's what I asked from those people. The situation was imposed and they couldn't consider someone who is a prisoner and who is helpless to be someone they could do what they liked with. This -- they had to understand that this would not be permitted because once you allow this kind of situation to escalate, prisoners will undergo great suffering. Not just here in this situation but throughout the war, at Ilidza, in the area there, company commander, a Muslim, was taken prisoner and he was beside himself because he thought this was the end. He thought he was going to lose his life. And I spoke to him and on the same day he was exchanged for someone else. So the treatment of prisoners had to be respectful and their lives had to be ensured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have the next time. You appointed Captain Simo Sipcic to co-ordinate the work between the civil organs and the army and between the military police and the civil police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the reason you did this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason was that I needed someone who was more familiar with the area than I was, and with the conditions there. In this case, Simo Sipcic was a person who was local. I don't know whether he was born there, but that's where he lived and worked, so he was the best person to act as co-ordinator and as a contact point. He let me know that he was willing to do this and I appointed him. I'm not saying I couldn't have chosen a better person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A hypothetical question, General: Would it have been easier for you if we had declared the state of war to introduce order or would the situation have been the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't need a state of war to be declared. What was necessary was for people to understand how they should conduct themselves because regardless of whether there was or was not a state of war, people went through the same thing. In the beginning it was impossible to appoint someone to do something and put him in a desired situation, but later on you could achieve that with everybody once they understood that without organised work and without a command there could be no successful defence, regardless of whether a state of war was declared or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this was an order to your subordinates. It was strictly confidential, of the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2829, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D7521, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a notice from you to the population, so it's a shorter version of what was in your order. Can you tell us what you informed the population about and why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something that is an integral part of the measures needed by the military organisation. There can be no defence, there can be no possibility of putting things right if the population starts leaving and so on. If there are civilian family members in the defence area, then those who are defending the area will defend it better if they know their family's there than if they know their family has left. So I wanted to restrict the movement of people in order to prevent the area from being depopulated. That was what I wanted to do, and I think that this was something that was part of the defence of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This second paragraph says that unauthorised persons are prohibited from entering abandoned and empty flats. This could be done only by the military police. And in the end, people are warned that there will be severe punitive measures.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In the area of Grbavica there was something called Digitron. That's where certain groups gathered until I managed to put them under control. They started asking me on whose side I was. They thought that we were communists who wanted to restore the old brotherhood and unity system. But later on, those same people came to understand that all this was in their interest and they all managed to fit in with the way that they were supposed to behave and they acted normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you refer to their behaviour towards Muslims and Croats in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm -- what I'm saying is that some people, when it comes to Muslims, thinking that I was only protecting Muslims and that I was working against the interest of those who were self-willed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2830, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we look at 1D7526.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One question for you, General. How was this notice notified to the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through certain local communes, representatives of the population. Through individuals in certain areas, in certain streets or neighbourhoods or parts of the town. So those were their civil representatives who were well-respected in their communities and it was up to them to communicate this to their neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in those local communes, were there any notice boards which could be used to put up notices?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course there were. I can't recall whether any of these notices were put up on the notice board, but I wanted it to be communicated to people in a closer way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D7526.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a combat report of the 10th of November, when you were already commander. It's a regular combat report in which you informed the Main Staff, the forward command post, and the two neighbouring corps of what the enemy is doing. So let's look at the bottom of the page where it says fire was opened on targets in depth and on infantry positions in the city. Can you explain what this means?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a consolidated, compiled report which has the purpose of informing the Main Staff of combat activities on the entire area. When it comes to the area that is outside the city, it was fired on in depth, whereas in the city only on positions which were in our immediate vicinity or in shelters, trenches, dug-outs, or fortifications which were directly in front of us without the depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that first instance, what did the enemy have in depth which was worth firing on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's quite clear, they can have artillery there. They can have reserve there, approaching units. They can have certain waiting areas for the bringing in of fresh forces, waiting for new tasks. So it depends on what you discover there, but basically it boils down to artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us in item 5, morale and security situation, the first three lines, can you read the sentence and tell us what this is about? "To all units ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see. I see. There's no need for me to read what it says here. We sent it to all the units, or rather, all the units were given a large number of copies of Law on the Application of the Law on Military Courts and the Law on Military Prosecutors' Offices During a State of War. I can see that now, that we were supposed to distribute this once a state of war was declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell Their Honours how the military justice system was organised in the area of the corps, what services were there and what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military justice system continued operating, it continued to exist, to the best of my understanding, in a similar way as in peace time. There were military courts, there was a military prosecutor, and there were organs engaged in doing this work. In -- as part of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, there was a legal service which had its chief and, I repeat, there were military courts and a military prosecutor's office doing everything that was done in other situations as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2831, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D7538.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting, General, how were military courts and prosecutors' offices allocated with respect to the military territorial situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the military court and military prosecutor's office were located in Ilidza. That's where they were and that's where that part of the judiciary was located. Further, there was a military court for the Republika Srpska, to the best of my knowledge, in Zvornik. It's quite certain that in other areas there were other military courts, but I can't confirm this although I know they must have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So did I understand correctly that the area of responsibility of a corps had its own military court and military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you interfere in the work of the military courts and military prosecutor? How did they conduct their jobs, if you know? Who could arrest a person and so on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I knew, although I didn't interfere. With the help of my own legal service and the security organ, I submitted criminal reports against persons who had done something unlawful. And to the best of my knowledge, there were about 70 criminal reports which I signed and submitted for further procedure. If there is an understanding that there was nothing further I could do, I could not prosecute or interfere, I maintain that I did my job to the best of my ability. I did not interfere with the work of the military courts. I did get First-Class Captain Jamina [phoen], who was a military prosecutor, to give instructions to officers in Grbavica and Ilidza to contact the soldiers to tell them what they could expect if they acted in an unlawful manner. He did this very conscientiously. I congratulate him on this. I'm not saying this was the only influence on the fighters. It was one of many influences for them not to commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you discussing the 70 criminal reports during your command, and in addition to that, were there any reports concerning misdemeanour and, if so, what were the figures in that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was discussing the criminal reports during the period of my command. I can't tell you anything about misdemeanours because they were of lesser importance at the time to me. I can't say what the figure was. I was only discussing the number of criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at item 5, please. There is some mention of four criminal reports against soldiers for the crime of theft within the AOR of the brigade. That was while you were still with the 1st Romanija Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it mean there was one soldier who committed four crimes of theft or four soldiers in a single theft?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, it wasn't a single soldier. There were four criminal reports against soldiers, plural, who had committed the crime of theft in the area of responsibility of the brigade. The reports will be passed on to the office of the military prosecutor for further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was already on the 4th of July, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can scroll up so that the General can see the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2832, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D7539?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for it, please tell us who is Lieutenant-Colonel Ljuban Kosovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Kosovac was assistant commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps for morale and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date is October 1992. Was Colonel Kosovac in the unit during your period there when you were the chief?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was the Chief of Staff he was the assistant commander for morale and legal affairs. I can't recall when he left exactly. I don't know if he was still there when I assumed my duties. I do know, though, that in the corps Colonel Dragicevic was in that position. He had taken over and it -- I seem to have a recollection that Kosovac by that time retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is Colonel Kosovac sending here? Did you in the brigade receive these guide-lines for determining the criteria for prosecution? Have a look at the first paragraph. Just tell us briefly what it's about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even without reading I know what he could have asked for. In this instance, as the competent organ, he provided guide-lines on how to behave and what measures to take to normalise the situation in the prevention of crime for the sake of unified policy relating to prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in addition to the crimes against the armed forces or avoiding draft calls, we also have property crime, profiteering, war crimes, et cetera; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The whole point was to have the forces act in the sense that war crimes should be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2833, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 1D07035.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, have a look, please. The date is the 15th of December, 1992. You are still in command of the 1st Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 2, maximum observation and so on. Does this tally with what you have told us previously that observation was an ongoing activity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That type of activity had to be in place at all times; however, here it is stated that it forms the basis of our guarantee of proper conduct. The system of observation, pin-pointing targets, following the movement of the enemy and its columns, all that was a precondition to protecting ourselves and in order to take action against such activity which threatens our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the next page and for the time being I would ask that it not be broadcast. Item 4 in the English, so that's the next page as well. I'm not certain whether it should be broadcast or not, but it is better to be cautious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In item 4 you report that on the 13th of December, at around 2200 hours, there was an incident resulting in a death, civilian Ilija Pavlovic was killed and it seemed that another civilian reported it who was Muslim. There are soldiers referred to, including Pavlovic who went to the apartment of a Muslim woman while drunk and that there was a risk that they would rape her. Mladen Janic and Glogovac and Buha and Ujic went to the flat. They found there the above-mentioned soldiers who were completely drunk and they escorted them to the company command. Can you discuss the following paragraph without referring to the names, please. It seems there was some shooting, too.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This reminds me of the last name of the person who took measures to prevent this. It was Mr. Glogovac, I believe, or someone. He knew what needed to be done, what was permitted, what was not. He prevented this situation, and thanks to him, it did not escalate to the point of a crime being committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Ibro person, I won't mention his last name, he was Muslim, and he reported it and his report was acted upon. That's what the document says?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It means that we trusted that there was something he wanted to report and followed up on his information. It was acted on professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we have to put it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2834, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you have any paramilitary units in the corps or in its area, especially as of the moment you became the chief and commander later on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any. Let me add this: I have to acknowledge General Galic's efforts. He acted emphatically in cutting off and removing all such elements. In that way he made my job easier, since I no longer had to deal with them anymore. Whatever there was, was under the command of the 1st and 3rd Sarajevo Brigades. There were no other kind of forces. When I say "the 1st and 3rd Sarajevo Brigades," I wanted to say that there were volunteers in their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the volunteers enjoy the same status, the same rights and obligations as the regular soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. Even more importantly, they were equal in the sense that they died equally. A Russian was killed, I even have the exact date of his death and what happened to him. There were situations where volunteers lost their limbs when they stepped on mines. I think it was even the same man. So they lived under the same conditions and engaged in the same activities as the other fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, was there uniformity in terms of dress as it had existed in the JNA and appearance? For example, were there people wearing beards? Were there soldiers or officers of yours who behaved, let's say, in an unconventional way, standing out in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to say very much so that it was not our priority, it was not a key matter to be followed. But it is true that in terms of dress and appearance they were all equal. However, some were not asked to shave their faces. That remained as the only characteristic which made them stand out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 15703.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the same apply to their hair and personal image? The date is the 27th of August, 1993. There you report on the measures undertaken regarding the Vaska case. What was it all about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Vaska, do you want me to read it all because we may lose time? Vaska stood out in terms of his appearance, he looked differently. He knew well, because I had told him that it was not appropriate and that he looked untidy. It didn't contribute one bit to his image. After several attempts to make him understand and after that failed, we took measures because he failed to realise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 1 you discuss his conduct towards UNPROFOR, and the document then states that Vaska was to follow what you had prescribed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had that streak in his behaviour and he had difficulty in understanding that it had nothing to do with military structures and civilised behaviour. The issue of respect of UNPROFOR and their mission, it was important to us, not only that it is respected by most of them but all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at item 3. It seems that the offences he had committed before were not forgotten. Please read it out.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Corps Command decided, for the time being, to file criminal charges against Vaska, make him responsible for the mistakes he had made previously -- hold him responsible ."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2835, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D7540.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you will conclude your examination-in-chief today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my utmost, Your Excellencies. Perhaps I will have a couple of minutes left for tomorrow -- actually, I could do it on the day of the cross, although I hope to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber needs to rise at quarter to 3.00 sharp, and I would like you to leave five minutes at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If I have a few documents left, would it be acceptable if I did it before the cross-examination starts on the day when it starts? This would avoid us having to re-call the General tomorrow. Or perhaps I can do it over one session tomorrow morning, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And there's no change as to the order of witnesses in terms of the agreement between the parties, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My understanding of the agreement is that the cross-examination of the General will be put forward to another date, but we haven't in the interim, as this testimony has gone on, finalised when that date might be precisely. Recalling Your Honour's indication about when you would prefer the cross-examination begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you are ready, I would like to hear it immediately following the examination-in-chief, but it doesn't seem to be the case. I would like you to start immediately following the conclusion of three witnesses' evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I can address that briefly, Mr. President, just that -- because I think I had discussions with Mr. Robinson about this. I know I did with someone and I thought it was with him. We were aware of the Trial Chamber's preference to -- aware both of the estimation that the witnesses who were expected to commence tomorrow -- and now it's coming back to me, I think I had this discussion after being notified yesterday that the Defence expected to take the entirety of the day today. We then expected to move on to the other witnesses. That order, of course, remained the same in terms of their appearance. And I simply -- and then we also acknowledged the Trial Chamber's preference to begin the cross-examination thereafter, and I simply put down a marker at that time that we were hoping to do just that and thought we could, but that if the examinations of the three witnesses who were expected to testify tomorrow did not last the entirety of the day, we nevertheless thought that the cross-examination of Mr. Milosevic should not begin until the earliest on Thursday. So that was the understanding. I didn't hear -- so that's kind of the minimum discussion that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That point has been taken. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please cast a glance. This was issued in December 1993. We will see at the end that Ljuban Kosovac, your assistant, i.e., Galic's assistant at the time, reported about the work of the military prosecutor's office and the military court, both tied to his corps. It is stated here that during that period of time before you became commander, 79 criminal reports were filed against 90 individuals. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I read. This is the information that was provided in the form of an analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what was the breakdown of crimes? You will find it in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crimes against property, violent crimes and other crimes. Violation of guard duty, for example, that would be the first. Assaulting military personnel, theft, murder, illicit trade, endangering public traffic, rape, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to broadcast this. We don't have to pronounce the names of the perpetrators, but I would like to go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, look at bullet point 9, paragraph 2. Could you please summarise it or maybe even read the whole of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bullet point 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, second paragraph below the name.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In order to take preventive action, the Military Prosecutor at the SRK Command visited some units of the Corps, and on that occasion, he informed the commands and relevant organs about the problems encountered in the work of the Military Prosecutor's Office ..." Basically, this is the gist of the problem for which I hired a military prosecutor as a person who played the role that he knew how to play and to influence other people's behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He mentions problems. He says that there are shortcomings in reports, there are difficulties in obtaining information, hindered work of law enforcement organs, poor communication, shortage of staff, difficult working conditions, and so on and so forth. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, were you aware of any case of either successful or unsuccessful cover-up of a crime by military prosecutors' offices or officers in your corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean when you say "cover up"? How should I be able to cover things up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not you. Was there anybody in your corps, any judicial organs in your corps that tried to cover up a crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such instances. I'm not aware of anybody's intentions of that kind or even successful attempts to do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the first page? While the content of this document referred to criminal reports by Ilidza Brigade, Ilijas Brigade, 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, why was it sent to -- only to 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade? Or was it sent to all brigades? But I don't see that notation from the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? The 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade in the meantime had already left the contingent of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. This is a document that was sent only to them. It is more than certain that there are other documents which were sent to all the commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2836, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, now I would like to draw your attention to the elements of command and control in the zone of responsibility of your brigade and then of your corps but in very general terms. Could you please tell us something about the ways of communication between units and their commands, especially the beginning of 1992? What was the status of communications, relays, telephones, and what was the accessibility of areas, places, by road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I managed to understand your question. My view of the system of command was this: The system of command can only function if they are supported by a good communications system. This is not the only condition for the good functioning of the system of command and control, but it is one of very important factors. The system of communications and its capacities are very important. Obviously, at first nothing worked properly. The biggest problem was the fact that the technical equipment that we had at our disposal was very obsolete. Those things, the equipment, radios, radio relay equipment, could be intercepted by anybody and that was a big problem for the system of command which needs to be established. There is another principle which is the principle of physical conduct, immediate contact, and commanding people. Roads were also important but it also played an obstacle in communication. The command role implies that everybody could receive orders, but this was impossible because of the distances, weak communications, and many other obstacles to that communication.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7527.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, do you remember Major Pera Jesic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know the major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an intercept of your telephone conversation which you had on the 24th of May, four days after the Army of Republika Srpska was established. This was recorded by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at pages 4 and 2 in Serbian and English respectively. This is not a good page in English -- no, it is, it is. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the Serbian page and see where it says: "Check if you have any communication with them ..." That's what you are asking?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I can see that and I'm asking him to tell me whether there is communication, whether they are in contact with them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the bottom he says: "We didn't get further away from Sokolac."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, he's talking about the interaction in communications, about the non-existence of communications, so he cannot get in touch with somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He says -- you ask: "So what is the situation over there in Rogatica? You don't know." So you didn't know what the situation was in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. And this is really good. Now it takes me back. This is a journey down memory lane. A company remained there, yes, this was a period that completely escaped me. When the brigade arrived, one company remained in the Mesici sector, which is in Rogatica. I wanted to know what was going on with that company because I could not reach them. I was not in contact with that company that I later on transferred and deployed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was the 216th, or rather, the 1st Romanija Brigade? That was on the 24th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We already said that it was in the territory of Sarajevo, i.e., it was in Vrace, Grbavica, one part of Tilava, in that area basically.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2837, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're still talking about command and control, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7528.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the reporting system? How did you report about activities and combat tasks? Who was it who compiled those reports? Were their authors professional officers and can you tell us something about all that and tie it to this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to read the document. I know what problems we encountered in our work. During that period of time and a bit later, the organs that collected information, who provided answers, and who were in command of their units, who were supposed to comply with rules and regulations that came from higher instances were not functioning properly, which is not surprising because nobody could do things properly from scratch. Nobody could be expected to be the best possible officer from day one. The system of command is very complex which is always repaired, improved, shortcomings are eliminated, so as to make sure that that system may function as well as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What are the most important conditions that need to be put in place in order to have a good system of command, including technical equipment and personnel?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are important. The most important thing is willingness to do things and seriousness in approach. People who were not trained, who did not have enough knowledge, can make up for the shortcomings if they were willing to learn. That was the prevailing intention for people to overcome their shortcomings through work and through learning from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the last page to see that it was delivered to the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade, the 1st Romanija Brigade, and that it was signed by Colonel Galic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The General specifically said he didn't want to read the document, so I don't know if he's given a basis for its admission. All that being said, though, I have no issue about the authenticity of the document, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I took that statement to mean that he agreed with the document. Given your position, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2838, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, while the document is still on the screen, this was issued on the 7th of September, 1992. Let's look at the situation as it was two months later. 1D7529. Take a look at the document, please, and then tell us what the document refers to. Are there still shortcomings in the system of reporting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sent by the corps command. The corps command sought ways to introduce order and rules into the system of reporting. The corps command needed to know exactly what was happening in particular areas. Shortcomings were again observed in the system of reporting. There were elements that the corps command needed to have. That's why they are requesting all the units to work on eliminating those shortcomings, and the main principle was to be accurate in the system of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2839, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 1D7532, to see what the situation was like eight months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this document? It was signed by you. It is a request to all brigades and the Vogosca Tactical Group.
